title: Programmable delivery of genetic therapies to most tissues

concept.text: The innovation would be a reusable, adaptable way to deliver therapeutic genetic payloads selectively and reliably to specified human cell populations across a broad range of tissues. Instead of developing an entirely new delivery vehicle for every target, a modular platform would allow components to be changed to reach the intended cells while preserving useful parts of the delivery system. Success would require reaching enough target cells to produce a therapeutic effect, with acceptable exposure elsewhere.

Intended targets include the central nervous system, muscle, and stem-cell compartments. These define the proposed scope; the supplied evidence documents a liver-directed example and does not establish delivery performance in those other compartments. The platform would provide access for genetic therapies, while the payload would still determine what happens inside the cells. Delivery, safe editing or reprogramming, and clinical benefit therefore remain distinct requirements.

A narrower technical basis for modularity appears in the supplied review of the May 2025 CPS1-deficiency case report. The article discusses the possibility of reusing the lipid nanoparticle formulation and messenger RNA while customizing the guide RNA for related hepatic therapies. That supports component reuse within liver-directed treatment; extending comparable programmability across organs remains the proposed breakthrough.

significance.text: Conditional synthesis: reliable access to difficult cell populations could make many otherwise suitable genetic therapies feasible. Reusable delivery components could also reduce the need to repeat vehicle development for every application. The revolutionary consequence would be a broadly useful enabling capability: more therapeutic payloads could be tested in the cells where they need to act. Neither faster development nor successful treatment across organs has been demonstrated by the supplied case.

The hepatic case provides a concrete reason to take reuse seriously: its discussion describes sharing delivery and editing components while changing the guide RNA. This is a useful starting point for a platform approach, although it does not show that a formulation can be redirected among substantially different tissues.

Conditional synthesis: broader delivery could support disease correction, immune-cell modification, or regenerative interventions when an effective payload and sufficient cell coverage are available. These possibilities depend on additional breakthroughs and disease-specific validation. A delivery platform would not itself guarantee accurate editing, controlled reprogramming, restored tissue function, or durable clinical benefit. Its value would also depend on acceptable immunity, toxicity, dosing, and practical treatment requirements.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unsolved capability is reusable control over which cells receive a genetic payload, at therapeutically sufficient coverage, across substantially different tissue environments. The engineering objective combines targeting, biodistribution, delivery efficiency, and therapeutic exposure. Reaching an organ is insufficient if too few of its relevant cells receive functional payload, or if unintended cells receive unacceptable exposure.

Proposed engineering barriers include avoiding unintended uptake, accommodating different payload sizes and formats, maintaining useful delivery efficiency, and limiting immune responses and toxicity. Central nervous system, muscle, and stem-cell delivery are intended challenges for the platform. The supplied study does not establish the specific barriers or present delivery status in those compartments, nor does it substantiate the general payload-capacity constraint. These remain design concerns requiring additional evidence rather than reasons to discard the concept.

The supplied article gives narrower grounding for immune and dosing concerns. Its discussion contrasts the potential for lipid nanoparticle re-dosing with immune constraints associated with AAV vectors, and the reported patient received two infusions. This supports treating immunity, repeat administration, and safety as substantive development questions. It does not establish that repeat dosing will remain safe and effective across different payloads, tissues, or longer treatment courses.

current_state.text: A report published on May 15, 2025, by Kiran Musunuru and colleagues described personalized in vivo base-editing treatment of an infant with carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase 1 deficiency, or CPS1 deficiency. The treatment used hepatocyte-directed lipid nanoparticles and was administered in two infusions. This demonstrates a personalized, liver-directed clinical application within the reported single-patient scope.

Over the reported seven-week observation period, the infant tolerated increased dietary protein and reduced nitrogen-scavenger use, with no serious adverse events reported. These are encouraging early clinical observations. They do not establish long-term efficacy or safety, and direct assessment of editing through liver biopsy was deferred. The clinical observations therefore should not be presented as direct measurements of editing in the patient's liver.

The article's proposal to reuse hepatic delivery and editing components is a prospective platform argument. The reported treatment does not demonstrate a general delivery system for other organs, durable benefit across multiple diseases, or coverage of most tissues.

Evidence scope: the supplied review assessed a verified saved artifact containing the complete main article, with no reported extraction truncation. The earlier account of a browser verification challenge therefore does not describe the evidence available for this assessment. Linked supplements and figure images were not supplied for inspection, so conclusions here are limited to the main-article findings described in the review.

Temporal limitation: the supplied materials establish this May 2025 result historically. They contain no freshness search establishing subsequent developments through November 1, 2026. Consequently, this record cannot establish the latest frontier or confirm that every part of the proposed capability remained unachieved at that later date.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed milestone: demonstrate a modular platform that delivers functional genetic payloads to therapeutically sufficient fractions of several distinct, previously difficult-to-target human cell types. Each application should define its required cell coverage, acceptable unintended exposure, clinically meaningful benefit, and follow-up period in advance. These are proposed evaluation criteria, not established consensus standards; the supplied evidence does not justify universal numerical thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Functional payloads reach therapeutic coverage across difficult human cell types

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: show that shared platform components can be retained across applications while targeting components are adapted, and document the changes required for each tissue and payload. Measure delivery and functional payload action separately from clinical outcomes, so that improved symptoms alone are not treated as proof of target-cell delivery or editing. Convincing evidence would include reproducible results across patients and applications, with independent replication where feasible.
completion_criteria.label: Adapted targeting retains shared components with reproducible functional delivery

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: demonstrate durable benefit across multiple diseases, repeat dosing where the intended treatment requires it, and sufficiently long safety follow-up to assess delayed harms. Define the supported payload classes, doses, administration routes, patient populations, manufacturing requirements, and known exclusions. These boundaries would distinguish a practically reusable platform from isolated successes.
completion_criteria.label: Durable benefit spans multiple diseases within defined platform boundaries

completion_criteria.text: Proposed breadth criterion: success in several difficult cell types would establish a substantial milestone, but would not by itself establish delivery to most tissues. That broader claim requires an explicit definition of tissue coverage, a justified denominator, and evidence covering the relevant diversity of cell populations. Finite demonstrations can establish tested breadth and stated limits; they cannot establish literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Most tissues are reached under justified coverage definitions and denominators

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: BME-05, Programmable living medicines that sense and respond inside the body, overlaps when genetic delivery installs or modifies a therapeutic cellular program. BME-02 concerns getting the payload into the intended cells; BME-05 additionally requires sensing, response, and control of living therapeutic behavior. BME-08, Reliable, antigen-specific immune tolerance, could intersect with immune management for genetic therapies, but selective delivery does not itself establish antigen-specific tolerance.

Roster-based synthesis: BME-11, Controlled regeneration of complex organs in the adult body, and BME-03, Reconstruction of a chronically severed spinal cord, could use targeted genetic payloads as components of a larger intervention. They still require organized tissue repair and functional recovery. BME-17, Minimally invasive assembly of functional tissue inside the body, concerns constructing tissue rather than delivering genetic instructions alone.

Roster-based synthesis: BME-01, Manufacturing transplantable human organs on demand, BME-06, Long-term banking of transplantable human organs, and BME-12, Reliable, scalable animal-to-human organ transplantation, address organ production, preservation, and transplantation respectively. Genetic delivery could potentially support particular steps in these workflows, but would not establish their separate manufacturing, storage, compatibility, or transplant outcomes. BME-09, Physiological extra-uterine support through extreme prematurity, likewise requires an integrated physiological support capability beyond cell targeting.

Roster-based synthesis: BME-10, Validated patient-specific models for testing treatments before use, could support evaluation of delivery and payload effects, while requiring its own predictive validation. BME-15, Accessible deep-body molecular imaging, and BME-18, Long-lived continuous sensing of multiple clinically useful biomarkers, could potentially help measure distribution or response; neither is equivalent to delivering a therapeutic payload. BME-07, A broadly effective early-warning test for lethal cancers, concerns detection rather than therapeutic access.

Roster-based synthesis: BME-04, A durable bidirectional neural interface for movement and sensation, BME-13, Durable autonomous artificial-organ replacement, and BME-16, Long-lived tissue-integrated interfaces for implants, focus on devices and their sustained interaction with the body. BME-14, Shelf-stable, broadly compatible replacement for critical blood functions, focuses on a replacement therapeutic product. Possible combinations with genetic delivery do not merge these distinct capabilities or their completion criteria.

The supplied evidence does not establish delivery performance or the specific barriers in central nervous system, muscle, and stem-cell compartments, or substantiate the general payload-capacity constraint.
A defensible definition and denominator for reaching most tissues remain unspecified.
Application-specific thresholds for target-cell coverage, unintended exposure, clinical benefit, repeat dosing, and follow-up remain to be defined.
Long-term efficacy, long-term safety, and direct measurement of editing in the treated infant are not established by the reported seven-week observations.
Linked supplements and figure images were outside the supplied review's inspected evidence.

brief.title: Genetic treatments delivered to chosen cells across the body
possible: People could receive genetic treatments aimed at chosen cells across most tissues, including the brain and muscles. A reusable delivery system would change its targeting parts for each application while keeping other components, reaching enough intended cells to make treatment work.
why: For patients, access to hard-to-reach cells could make more genetic treatments feasible. For developers, reusable delivery components could reduce the need to build a new carrier for every treatment.

sources.showed: They treated an infant with a rare genetic disease using lipid nanoparticles, tiny fat particles carrying gene-editing tools to liver cells. The infant tolerated more dietary protein and less medicine for removing nitrogen.
sources.quote: In the 7 weeks after initial treatment, he tolerated increased dietary protein and nitrogen scavenger reduction despite viral illnesses.
sources.cited_for: This demonstrates a personalized genetic treatment directed at the liver.
sources.not_established: It does not establish lasting benefit, directly measured liver editing, or delivery across different organs.

sources.showed: They attached antibodies, proteins that bind selected targets, to fat particles carrying messenger RNA, instructions for making proteins. The particles targeted T cells, an immune cell type, in mice and selected human immune cells outside the body.
sources.quote:
These precisely targeted LNPs
showed highly efficient in vivo targeting to T cells, with minimal delivery
to other immune cells.
sources.cited_for: Changing attached antibodies offers a way to adapt delivery to different cell targets.
sources.not_established: It does not establish therapeutic benefit or reliable delivery across diverse human tissues.

sources.who: Qin Huang, Ken Y Chan, Benjamin E Deverman and colleagues
sources.showed: A redesigned viral shell, or capsid, delivered genes across the central nervous system (CNS), the brain and spinal cord, in mice carrying a human binding protein. It also crossed human cells forming the barrier between blood and brain.
sources.quote: one capsid crossed the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and mediated efficient CNS-wide gene delivery.
sources.cited_for: This demonstrates a route toward gene delivery throughout the brain.
sources.not_established: Delivery in genetically altered mice does not establish effective brain delivery in human patients.

sources.who: Rohan Palanki, John S Riley and colleagues
sources.showed: Targeted fat particles delivered gene-editing tools to fetal blood-forming stem cells, which produce blood cells. Injection before birth produced editing in mice.
sources.quote: Finally, we showed that optimized and targeted LNPs enhanced gene editing at a proof-of-concept locus in fetal HSCs after a single in utero intravenous injection.
sources.cited_for: This demonstrates delivery and editing in a difficult stem-cell population before birth.
sources.not_established: It does not establish treatment of human blood disease or access to adult blood-forming stem cells.

shown: Musunuru and colleagues reached clinical treatment in a single infant, with early improvements and no serious adverse events reported. Chen, Huang and Palanki and their colleagues demonstrated targeted delivery to immune cells, the brain and fetal blood-forming cells in separate experimental systems.
missing: A shared delivery system has yet to reach enough intended cells across substantially different human tissues while limiting exposure elsewhere.
Adapted targeting has yet to produce reproducible results across patients and applications while retaining shared components.
A reusable platform has yet to deliver lasting benefit across diseases, with safe repeat dosing where needed and follow-up for delayed harms.

milestones.label: Enough hard-to-reach human cells receive working genetic material
milestones.explanation: A modular system would have to deliver working genetic material to enough cells of several difficult human cell types, with acceptable exposure elsewhere. This would establish useful reach.

milestones.label: Changed targeting preserves shared parts and reproducible delivery
milestones.explanation: Adapted targeting would have to retain shared components and reproducibly demonstrate delivery and action inside cells across patients and applications. This would establish reuse beyond symptom improvement.

milestones.label: Lasting benefit across diseases within clear treatment limits
milestones.explanation: Treatments would have to show lasting benefit across diseases, repeat dosing where needed, and follow-up for delayed harms within stated operating limits. This would establish practical reuse.

milestones.label: Most tissues reached under a justified definition
milestones.explanation: Results would have to cover most tissues under an explicit, justified definition of which tissues and cell populations count. This would establish breadth beyond several difficult targets.

uncertain: What fraction of intended cells must receive treatment, and how much unintended exposure is acceptable, will depend on the application.
Which tissues and cell populations should count when judging whether delivery reaches most tissues?
The treated infant's long-term safety and benefit remain unknown, and editing in the liver was not directly measured.

page.title: Programmable in vivo delivery of genome editors
page.definition: A delivery system can be modified through a known biological mechanism to deliver DNA-editing machinery to at least three distinct cell types, tissues or organs inside the body. Delivery and editing meet published target-specific efficiencies and undergo independent validation in large animals.

goal.need: ARPA-H estimated on 25 September 2025 that rare diseases affect over 30 million Americans and roughly 95% have no approved treatments. Its THRIVE programme combines gene-correcting tools with cell-targeted delivery. These figures describe the overall rare-disease burden; the announcement does not estimate how many patients would benefit from programmable genome-editor delivery.

figures.caption: Rare-disease treatment gap reported by ARPA-H on 25 September 2025
figures.note: The estimates cover rare diseases collectively.

statements.body: National Institutes of Health, Somatic Cell Genome Editing programme
statements.quote: Be programmable and target at least three distinct and different cell(s), tissue types, and/or organs.
statements.context: A requirement for Target Area 1 of the TARGETED Challenge.

statements.body: Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, THRIVE programme
statements.quote: THRIVE intends to develop integrated platform technologies to accelerate precision genetic medicines (PGMs)

completion.title: Independent large-animal testing validates one delivery system across at least three distinct targets.
completion.criterion: NIH-supported independent testing demonstrates delivery and editing by one programmable system in at least 3 distinct cell types, tissues or organs in large animals, and NIH judges it to meet TARGETED Target Area 1. Delivery and editing must match or exceed published target-specific efficiencies. The system must demonstrate its targeting mechanism, biodistribution, administration route and a safety profile consistent with other delivery systems intended for human gene therapy.
completion.set_by: NIH TARGETED Challenge, Target Area 1 final requirements and Phase 3b evaluation; revision of 2 July 2025.
completion.threshold_quote: demonstration of delivery and editing in at least three different cell types, tissues, and/or organs.
completion.basis: This is a published preclinical test of programmability. FDA makes therapeutic editing thresholds depend on indication and patient population. NIH's three-target scope supplies a defined breadth test; it does not define “most tissues” or establish human benefit.

milestones.title: Modifying a delivery system redirects functional cargo delivery through an identified biological mechanism.
milestones.criterion: Changing the carrier changes cellular targeting through an explained biological mechanism. With anti-CD3-targeted lipid nanoparticles, Chen et al. observed a fluorescent marker in 50% of splenic CD4+ and 54% of splenic CD8+ T cells, 24 hours after delivery of 0.1 mg/kg mRNA encoding Cre recombinase in 6 mice. With adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors, Huang et al. reported 40–50-fold greater central nervous system reporter expression with BI-hTFR1 than AAV9 in mice expressing human transferrin receptor (4 versus 3 mice; 3 weeks). The AAV experiment measured gene delivery, without delivering a genome editor.
milestones.set_by: NIH TARGETED Challenge, Phase 2 programmable-mechanism requirement.
milestones.threshold_quote: Demonstrate the programmable mechanism: provide data showing delivery to different targets

milestones.title: A delivery system delivers an active genome editor that changes DNA in its intended cells in vivo.
milestones.criterion: The delivered editor changes DNA in intended cells inside the body. Palanki et al. found approximately 8% versus 2% editing at the TTR locus in blood-forming stem cells isolated from fetal mouse liver, 5 days after intravenous dosing at 1 mg/kg mRNA on embryonic day 13.5 (reported minimum n=3). Separately, Musunuru et al. treated 1 infant with carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase 1 deficiency using 2 liver-directed infusions; the 7-week report found increased protein tolerance and reduced nitrogen-scavenger treatment, but no liver biopsy measured editing.
milestones.set_by: NIH TARGETED Challenge, Phase 2 editing-capacity criterion.
milestones.threshold_quote: Demonstration of the editing capacity for genome editing machinery within the delivery system.

milestones.title: One delivery technology demonstrates delivery and editing in at least three distinct target configurations.
milestones.criterion: One technology has at least 3 target configurations, with proof of concept and comparative editing performance. Cheng et al. reported liver-, lung- and spleen-specific CRISPR editing with selective organ targeting (SORT) lipid nanoparticles in mice: 3 mice/group; liver and lung, 2.5 mg/kg total RNA and 10-day readout; spleen, 4 mg/kg and 2-day readout. NIH announced Phase 2 awards for AAV vectors, engineered virus-like particles and milk exosomes on 12 May 2025; the announcement provides no target-level measurements and is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: NIH TARGETED Challenge, Phase 2 minimum of three configurations and comparative-editing requirement.
milestones.threshold_quote: at least three different cell types, tissues and/or organs

milestones.title: A delivery system produces sterile test reagents with endotoxin at most 0.5 EU/mL.
milestones.criterion: In vivo studies justify dose and administration route for large-animal evaluation, and scaled reagents pass testing-centre sterility and endotoxin acceptance at ≤0.5 endotoxin units/mL. NIH permits intravenous or intramuscular injection. Zempleni's university CV lists a $50,000 Phase 3a award for programmable milk exosomes covering 1 July 2025 to 30 August 2026; this administrative record is not peer-reviewed performance data or evidence that a batch passed acceptance.
milestones.set_by: NIH TARGETED Challenge, Phase 3 readiness and testing-centre reagent acceptance; revision of 2 July 2025.
milestones.threshold_quote: verify sterility and endotoxin level (≤0.5 EU/ml)

not_found: No definition or tissue denominator for “most tissues” was found in NIH TARGETED rules, FDA genome-editing guidance or ARPA-H THRIVE materials.
No public completed TARGETED Target Area 1 independent large-animal validation dataset or final award was located through 14 November 2026.
No public testing-centre batch-acceptance measurements for the cited Phase 3a milk-exosome project were located.
